title: Teaching in New Iberia, then Los Angeles with Wingy Manone, Mercer and Ory
summary: Reason teaches music and does a radio show, goes to California, gets into Local 47 through Manone, works for Johnny Mercer, and writes arrangements for Kid Ory.

story.theme_name: Going west: California and the Los Angeles scene
story.community_name: Going west: moving to and working in California

blocks.x: I met you there. We were in music school together. Yeah.

And, um, I was interested in going there because I wanted to take up, um, a, a stuffy stuff They haven't had another lesson since then and they raised their own family and just from what I taught them they became a professional musician. So I see them now, they wanted to call me, they didn't know whether they should call me Mr. Reason. I see that, so one boy by the name of Joe Dutry said, I tell you we're going to call him Pops. And I started those boys off and one of the boys, the little white boy, the young fellow must have been about 15, 15, 16 years old. I taught him clarinet. And when the next year, he was an exceptional student and he went to school here.

at LSU and he made first chair. And he told me that the instructor didn't believe he took music lessons in Liberia. So his daddy said I told him it wasn't New Iberia, it was the man who was teaching it. His name was Aban. Your school and the quality of your teaching. Yeah. And the home, I rented a six room house on Madison Slew. And the man who owned the house sold the house without telling me he was going to sell it. And so I moved to a small single house and I stopped teaching. And I just kept a few students. Then I became the disc jockey for a program over KVIM in New Iberia, Louisiana. And some of my students that I taught to encourage them on Saturday mornings at 10 o'clock, I would have them on live. They were youngsters, 18, 18, 12. I'd have them to play and sing. It was just an impromptu show. And when this was, while I was doing that, I went back to work to play at a place called the Victory Club. Well, the club owner came and asked me why was I throwing my time away when I could be making $300 or $400 a week. So I went over there and started working with him. And then I kept my little evening show because that was just one hour, four to five until I decided I wanted to go to California. So I went down to California. And I went to Los Angeles. The same week I got there, I joined the Local 47. And they earned, it was $150 to join the union. So I gave them $150 and my transfer card. And they told me I had to wait 90 days before I could go to work regular. And I could do casuals. And I used to go down to the union every day. And you could get a reservation through one of the rehearsal rooms. And I went out practicing. One day I was practicing. I never forget I was playing our arrangement on. I ain't got nobody. And a wingy man on. You ever hear of you? Oh yeah. I met him. Well, he looked, he opened the door. Look at that night. He said, hey cousin. I said, I heard that music out there. I ain't waiting around here like that. He said, where are you working? I said, I'm not working anymore. I'm supposed to wait 90 days. Only thing I can pay is a casual. So he said, come on with me. And at that time the president of the union was President Tigroy. And he took me upstairs. And he made me acquainted with the president. And he called him. He said, look, he said, this is my cousin from New Orleans. He said, I want him in my band. And so Tigroy asked him, he said, what's the gentleman's name? He said, he's no gentleman. He's a musician. He said, he said, well, how long has this musician been in town? And then he said, well, he been in a few weeks. So the president told him, he said, I didn't hear that. I don't want to hear it. He said, tell my secretary to come in here and bring his card with him. He took my card. He tore it up. And he gave me another card. And that meant I had been in Los Angeles over two years. And I had been doing other work. And I had been doing other work. This was off the record. Doing other work, working with my cousin in a restaurant. So I went to work with Wingy. Then Wingy saw about my town. Put me in the band. Jack T. Gordon was in the band. I can't remember the other fellas. And he made me the leader of his band. And he took me down to Johnny Mercy's office. And he told Johnny Mercy's office. He said, I brought this New Orleans man here with me. He said, he's piano playing my band. He writes a lot of songs. He said, I want you to do something for him. So Johnny said, well, right now, he said, I'm tired up. And my health is not too good. He said, I'm fixing to go over to Hawaii. He said, I'm going to be over there for a few weeks. And when I come back, he said, I'll give you a call. And when I was on my way out, his lieutenant, I can't remember his name. And he said, leave your telephone number and address here with the secretary. And about two hours after I got home, the telephone rang. There was Johnny Mercy on the phone. He said, I didn't want to do business with you through Winky Men Home. He said, you're a writer. You don't need to go through anybody. So he gave me an appointment to come back. And I went back to his office and talked to him. So he gave me a job checking compositions. And he said, I'm going to go through the office. But people would write. They'd bring them. They always wanted Johnny Mercy to check the song. And he wasn't interested in that anymore. He had the Palm Springs Publishing House then. And so he said, everything that doesn't look good, throw it in 513. Try his best. And so he advised me. He said, now we have a lot of folks come here with songs. They're not written right. They're, they are, some of them are too long to be commercial. He said, the secretary will give them your home number and let them go to your house. Then you can rewrite the song for them. Then you'll be part of the song. So I did, I started doing that. And I still worked in the band with Johnny. With Winky Men Home. And so, Winky carried me all over. He got pictures, everything done for me. And he told me about Kiddowry. Having a contract for the Benny Goodman story. And he said, Kiddowry needs you. You don't need him, but he needs you. Because some of the fellas had quit. And, did you ever meet Don Mule? E-W-E-L-L. Do you know him? Sure. Well, he had quit. Ory. And I went to work with Ory. When I got there, they brought me the same story that King Oliver gave me. We lost our music in the fire. We need you to write that stuff over. So, Ory hummed whole arrangements to me. That's the kind of memory Kiddowry had. Hummed the trumpet part. The clarinet part. And I set my piano at my little, I had a little, one room apartment up on 226 and a half, East 69th Street. And, uh, I bought a, uh, used piano for $25 and had it tuned up. And I used that for my practice and to, for these compositions. And Ory sat at the piano. And, uh, uh, uh, he hung these parts to me. And I make the arrangements for them. Then we recorded for Good Times Yes.
